blogs.title: When Threats Aren’t Persecution: The 10th Circuit’s Precise Stipulations on Past Persecution
blogs.description: This post examines the court’s insistence that threats alone cannot meet the INA’s definition of persecution, contextualizing the judgment with key cases such as Karki v. Holder and Wiransane v. Ashcroft. It delves into how cumulative psychological harm is weighed against the standard of “offensive” suffering, and what this means for future asylum applicants who rely on a spate of threats rather than concrete violence. The analysis also highlights the implications this decision has for U.S. immigration adjudicators attempting to balance evidentiary thresholds with the humanitarian purpose of asylum.

blogs.title: Political Opinion: Central, Peripheral, or Non‑existent? The Nexus Requirement Unpacked
blogs.description: Focusing on the court’s treatment of the nexus test, this piece explores the distinction between a protected ground that is a ‘central reason’ for persecution versus a tangential motive. It uses the Jimenez case to illustrate how the court allowed the BIA to find that the perpetrators’ actions were rooted in retaliation over a legal dispute rather than political ideology. The post compares this with precedent such as Dallakoti v. Holder and Laird v. Calef, offering a roadmap for litigants on how to effectively argue a political nexus when multiple motivations exist.

blogs.title: Can the Colombian State Protect Its Nuqueris? Scrutinizing the ‘Unable or Unwilling’ Standard
blogs.description: This blog explores the court’s rigorous application of the ‘unable or unwilling’ government protection test, drawing on the discussion in the opinion and related authorities like Aviles‑Gonzalez v. Garland. It dissects how the lack of a formal police report, the nature of local law‑enforcement interactions, and the evidentiary burden on the applicant converge to create a narrow path for proving state inability. The piece also considers the policy ramifications for asylum applicants claiming domestic security failures in countries with fragile law‑and‑order environments.

blogs.title: Safe Relocation in the Shadow of the Lore: How the 10th Circuit Leverages Internal Migration to Deny Asylum
blogs.description: Here we analyze the court’s application of the safe‑relocation exception, focusing on the record that the petitioners had relatives and family resources in unaffected Colombian regions. The post expands on how courts distinguish between mere geographic relocation and a ‘fundamental change’ in circumstances, referencing Rivera‑Barrientos and other circuits’ rulings. It also discusses the broader trend of courts tightening safe‑relocation standards and its impact on applicants from countries plagued by localized violence.
